final_proof:
Let the two sequences of observations be
\[
 a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n),\qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_n),
\]
and write
\[
 \bar a=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n a_k,
 \qquad
 \bar b=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n b_k.
\]
Because \(\mathbf C\) is asserted to be their (Pearson) correlation matrix, its entries must be defined. Thus both sequences have nonzero variance, equivalently
\[
 S_a:=\sum_{k=1}^n(a_k-\bar a)^2>0,
 \qquad
 S_b:=\sum_{k=1}^n(b_k-\bar b)^2>0.
\]
(If either sequence is constant, the corresponding Pearson correlations are undefined, so there is no correlation matrix of the stated kind.)

Set \(x^{(1)}=a\), \(x^{(2)}=b\), and let \(\bar x^{(i)}\) denote the mean of \(x^{(i)}\). By definition, for \(i,j\in\{1,2\}\),
\[
 C_{ij}
 =\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n
       (x^{(i)}_k-\bar x^{(i)})(x^{(j)}_k-\bar x^{(j)})}
      {\displaystyle
       \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^n(x^{(i)}_k-\bar x^{(i)})^2}
       \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^n(x^{(j)}_k-\bar x^{(j)})^2}}.
\]
Any common sample- or population-normalizing factors in the covariance and variances cancel, so this formula covers either convention.

Interchanging \(i\) and \(j\) leaves the numerator unchanged, by commutativity of multiplication, and merely interchanges the two factors in the denominator. Hence
\[
 C_{ij}=C_{ji}
\]
for every \(i,j\), and therefore \(\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf C\): the matrix is symmetric.

Finally, taking \(j=i\) gives
\[
 C_{ii}
 =\frac{\sum_{k=1}^n(x^{(i)}_k-\bar x^{(i)})^2}
        {\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^n(x^{(i)}_k-\bar x^{(i)})^2}
         \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^n(x^{(i)}_k-\bar x^{(i)})^2}}
 =1,
\]
because the sum of squares is positive. Thus every main-diagonal entry of \(\mathbf C\) equals \(1\), as claimed.
